sources.citation: WALS Online (local CLDF): Lugbara [lug], sources Anderson-1986, Barr-1965, Crazzolara-1960, Nichols-1992, Stolz-1996, Tucker-and-Bryan-1966.
sources.note: Lugbara has no values for the stress chapters 14A-17A (77 values in other chapters).

sources.citation: Crazzolara 1960, full 406-page scan (archive.org studyoflogbarama0000craz, print-disabled/lending only) probed through Open Library / Internet Archive full-text search-inside (AND queries anchored on the word 'Atsooli', p. 6).
sources.note: Positive controls ('Atsooli syllable', 'Atsooli lengthened', 'Atsooli stressed', 'Atsooli stressing') return the book; 'Atsooli stress', 'Atsooli accent', 'Atsooli accented', 'Atsooli emphasis', 'Atsooli prominence', 'Atsooli loud(ness)' and 'Logbara stress' return 0 hits, i.e. the tokens stress/accent occur nowhere in the book. The only 'stressed'/'stressing' fragments are emphatic forms and the emphasis particle: "'da stressed 'da!a, av. there, yonder;... (if not stressed at all 'da)", "'a or preferably stressed 'ale inside", 'less stressing of the demonstrative determinative is intended. F…

sources.citation: Crazzolara, J. P. 1960. A Study of the Logbara (Ma'di) Language: Grammar and Vocabulary. London: Oxford University Press for the International African Institute. xvii+373 pp. Ch. 1 'Sounds' (pp. 1-8) and ch. 2 'Intonation' (pp. 9-13); introduction §7 p. viii.
sources.access_detail: copy on file; access check: HathiTrust digitized, search-only (in copyright); interlibrary loan
sources.note: Nothing. The phonology and 'Intonation' chapters (read in full from the Rosetta Project scan of pp. 1-13) describe tone only: three marked tone levels (high/mid/low) plus combined tones, 'actually five distinct tone levels' (§53, p. 11), tone rules for verbs and inter-tonic reaction. Dialect basis: 'the dialect spoken around Arua... i.e. the dialect of the Aivu and Padzulu' (p. viii). The contents entries 'Stressing of Verbs §§426-30 p. 96' and 'The stressing ni §§561-71 p. 142' concern emphasis, not prosodic stress.

sources.citation: Hartell, Rhonda L. (ed.). 1993. Alphabets of Africa. Dakar: UNESCO / SIL. Lugbara page.
sources.note: Phoneme/grapheme chart only; 'Tones: high mid low'; nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Andersen, Torben. 1986. Tone splitting and vowel quality: evidence from Lugbara. Studies in African Linguistics 17(1): 55-68. doi:10.32473/sal.v17i1.107492
sources.note: Nothing on stress (grep stress/accent = 0). Eastern (Terego, Uganda) Lugbara has three level tones; Western (Zaire) Lugbara four; tone split conditioned by ATR.

sources.citation: Crothers, J. H., J. P. Lorentz, D. A. Sherman & M. M. Vihman (eds.). 1979. Handbook of Phonological Data from a Sample of the World's Languages (Stanford Phonology Archive). Entry 145 Logbara (Ma'di, Arua), pp. 77-78.
sources.note: Second-hand only: 'STRESS: Tucker and Bryan report that stress location varies among languages of the Moru-Ma'di group (which includes Logbara). Moru: stress on first syllable of disyllables. Ma'di: stress on final syllable.' Nothing for Logbara itself; three level tonemes, 'domain of tone: mora'.

sources.citation: Tucker, A. N. & M. A. Bryan. 1966. Linguistic Analyses: The Non-Bantu Languages of North-Eastern Africa. London: OUP for IAI. Ch. 'The Moru-Mangbetu languages', sec. 2a Tone / 2b Stress, p. 31.

sources.harvard_location: WID Old Widener 2235.4.26; LIN GEN CoPh 36.88
sources.note: Group level only: 'No such uniformity of stress pattern, however, has been found in the other Language Groups. Even such intimately closely allied languages as MORU and MA'DI have quite different stress behaviour' (Moru initial, Ma'di final). LUGBARA is named only under 2a Tone ('three tone levels have been established'); nothing on Lugbara stress.
